Content:
Honey isn’t the problem—affiliate networks are. They don’t offer a way for merchants to exclude coupon clicks, and that’s why influencers are losing commissions. If you’re an influencer or affiliate, I’d highly recommend using ReferZone and getting your merchants on board. Unlike other networks, ReferZone verifies whether a coupon was actually used before awarding commission to coupon sites—if not, the influencer gets full credit. If anyone knows other networks that offer this, LET ME KNOW.

Honestly, I’m shocked that so many in the industry, even top influencers, haven’t caught on. They can sue Honey and PayPal all they want, but it won’t fix the real issue. If they don’t switch to a platform that can actually deprioritize or exclude coupon clicks, they’re fighting the wrong battle.

Author: @SOEgame
Content:
Dude, I understand what you're going for with the Enron comment, but like, knowing a lot about the Enron scandal, it's really two completely different things. Enron was hiding billions of dollars of debt through outright fraud, fraud directed at their own shareholders. Honey is screwing over everyone who doesn't own Paypal, which is actually kind of a business strategy itself these days, and Honey is kind of just a side arm of the behemoth that is Paypal's financial service core. For this to compare to Enron, Paypal would have to basically be Sam Bankman-ing the funds they hold on behalf of customers, and hiding that fact on their balance sheets to both shareholders and the SEC. Jeffrey Skilling went to prison along with several other executives because of how audacious their accounting fraud was. This has nothing to do with accounting, and Honey was apparently widely profitable, as opposed to a black hole money pit that was Enron. Why would any accountants even sweat a bead at this? Its just another expense line item to them, and chances are pretty good that, unless something truly radical happens, Honey will still be a net profit in the end. All the accountants have to do about this is cut a check to their lawyers. Their lawyers might be panicking a bit, assuming they weren't already prepared for this day, because they fucked over a bunch of people not bound by an arbitration agreement. 

It's kinda more like Microsoft getting sued over One Drive, or MS Teams, like sure it'll be a hit and might hurt a bit, but they could easily lose that arm of the business and go about doing their normal thing, in this case, returning to seizing random Paypal entire accounts for made up reasons they never have to provide.

Author: @sagesight3602
Content:
I will say, I think you give LMG a bit too much credit with them not catching on. They're channels have been hacked three times, and while I may be making this next part up (can't remember specific instances off the top of my head), they've had other issues surrounding cyber security. I know there was a whole thing with them being dishonest about some product reviews at one point, but I don't know the specifics, as they were before I started watching them, and didn't look too deep into them.

Imo, LMG is a not good authority for cybersecurity issues/scams, though they have made a few good videos on good tech practices, such as not using public charging ports or cables found outside, using flash drives that you haven't been able to verify the origin/legitimacy of, etc.

Like you said, they also switched to another company doing something similar to honey immediately following breaking partnership with honey, which shows that, at best (honestly less sure, given that the lack of vocalization they made about the issue. Makes me worry for something more shady may be going on), they didn't take any precautionary or investigative measures into Karma, to see if they were also doing these types of things.

LMG, from an external perspective, doesn't seem to have awareness for these types of things.

Unrelated, but I'm mostly not surprised that this happened with honey, to be honest. There is truth to the saying that if it's too good to be true, it probably is. 

Every company that pops up like honey always seem to go something like this with their advertising "Use us, save money, no strings attached", but if you think about that for a little bit, and I hope I'm not alone in this, it becomes pretty clear that that makes no sense. From a business standpoint, their advertised business model is essentially, we give you money/spend money to save you money, and take nothing in return. Even if they were non-profit, they need to have a source of income, which that model has none. In fact, on paper, they would actively be losing money.

In that situation, maybe we can speculate they go to the company selling the products/coupons, and provide a service in exchange for the coupons/a portion of the profits, but then it becomes a question of what service would honey be providing to companies and/or how much of a profit stake would they take, and even moreso, since coupons, I feel like could be considered complimentary in financial transactions (in this context, referencing them most of the time being the least significant), would the income generated by this type of model really be enough for honey to have gotten as big as it is, as fast as it has.

Either way, that's only speculation, and what the known facts imply is that the product, from the side that is shown to consumers, doesn't make sense, unless there is something happening behind the scenes, the product's manufacturer (manufacturer may be wrong word here, but in this case, honey) hasn't told us about, in which case, at least two more questions need to be asked: Why? and: Where is the product manufacturer's revenue coming from?

For myself, if a product or company doesn't show clear answers to those questions, I don't trust them, because if they aren't willing to be upfront with the foundations of their business model, who knows what kinds of things they could be exploiting from their users with their knowledge or consent, to be in the green.

My first guess usually is that they're scraping user data and selling it to data brokers or other companies, and while I wouldn't be surprised if companies like honey were still doing this also, the one part of this that does surprise me somewhat with this is that honey has gone as far as to commit fraud.

but to touch on what charlie said near the start, yes, honey better be ready for one massive ass lawsuit because dozens if not hundreds of creators should be getting with their lawyers and filing a class action suit for well above millions of dollars in theft. if anything i believe they should sue for 70 million and let honey try to talk them down some. that way honey gets hit and will likely have to shut down, and the content creators/websites get a lot of their money back

Content:
That sounds absolutely fucking criminal. Like how do you not get classified as malware, if your program is meant to steal sales commissions off any purchase made on any browser with your software installed? That's screams fraud and white collar crime so hard it's unreal. The money they make this way is not generated out of thin air. It is stolen. And if the customer is there without being referred by a sponsored creator? Then it is stolen from the store who now pays part of the sale to Honey for just injecting their own link at the last split second. And why this is harmful apart from scamming the store in question? It means that less budget is left over to pay for the actual sales commissions. It means the products have to be priced higher to get any profit margins. And now everyone is paying more, because Honey is sneakily siphoning money into their own accounts.

Author: @twisted8ight
Content:
What I can't believe is how they could go this long before getting caught. 
I was very skeptical to this when I first started seeing the marketing. After a while, I installed the extension just to check it out, but I ended up deleting it again without even buying anything.

I'm not sure how non-influencers or "consumers" were scammed though. Afaik people still got lower prices, even though Honey intentionally didn't make specific codes available due to agreements with certain stores. And I haven't seen anything about profiting off of user data, although that might still be the case, who knows. 
Those that really got screwed here were influencers.
I can't help but feel there is some lack of due diligence here. I don't mean that influencers should be able to figure out the cookie swap themselves or anything, but I would think that they at least checked out what they were selling. And if you're paid thousands of dollars for giving them an ad, but you can't easily see how they are making the money to pay you that, some alarm bells should be going off imo. Just because some one else is doing something doesn't mean you should too.

The reason I didn't want to use Honey, was because I was sure they were feeding off of me some how, like selling my data or something like that.
And that idea was deemed okay by pretty much any influencer on here (except Markiplier and maybe some others) and they all gladly took the money for the ad, thinking their viewers where the once paying the bill. Turns out if was the influencers themselves paying for it.

I'm really interested in seeing this go to court, although it will likely never get there. I'm not even sure you could actually say that this is illegal. Honey got the last click after all.
Sure it's unfair to the content creator maybe, but I don't see how that matters to be quite honest. I'm sure PayPal must have done their due diligence on a $4B purchase though, so it's probably legal. I'd also looove to see one of the contracts for doing the honey-ad, that could get interesting.

Content:
Honestly, I don’t think the Honey thing is as bad as people are making it out to be. No one’s really losing here. Honey built the app, got the companies on board, and even lets affiliates put their links in—at the end of the day, it’s their infrastructure, so they can technically do what they want.

Yeah, hijacking commissions is a bit scummy, but it’s not illegal. They’re a business, not a charity, and let’s be real—PayPal owns Honey. If this was going to cause some massive legal mess, you think PayPal would let it happen? They’ve got entire teams of lawyers making sure this is airtight.

At worst, it’s just shady tactics, not some big scandal. Users still save money, Honey profits, and influencers move on. It’s Honey playing the game smarter, not some catastrophic fraud case.

Author: @tridekphlix3445
Content:
Doubt this comment will actually be properly noticed but I work in tech, and the video makes Honey seem like a scam, but it’s really just following the same rules that have applied across the entire internet for years now. Online advertising uses a “last click” system, where the last interaction before checkout gets the credit for a sale. For example, if you click a YouTuber’s affiliate link but later click a Google ad, Google gets the credit. Honey works the same way when it applies discount codes—it becomes the “last click.”

A lot of the frustration seems to come from people just now learning how this system works and blaming Honey because it’s the most visible example and don’t understand that this is just how it works everywhere.

I agree the system could be better. One idea might be for influencers to use unique codes at checkout, ensuring they get credit directly. But the current “last click” model exists for a reason, because it’s simple and scalable, even if it’s not perfect. The issue isn’t Honey—it’s the system itself, which at the end of the day, needs some kind of standard simple enough to properly scale across the entire internet.

Author: @voidler
Content:
I work in this space and it's not new at all nor is it a scam

Affiliates need to be picked for your program. The scenario needs to be that Linus AND Honey need to be on the affiliate program for that advertiser, and the user needs Honey installed. Although this could cause a problem it's exceedingly rare.

If only Linus is in the program then he will be awarded the sale, Honey is not in the program to be awarded any money

I very rarely saw Honey included in affiliate programs I've worked on because they don't add additional value to the purchase

I don't agree replacing UTMs are a problem - this is very common. Which is why individuals are still assigned to manually review the tracking to purchase in affiliate programs to identify any issues.

Another scenario that pops up frequently is that when users pay with PayPal, they are taken offsite before coming back. The purchase is then attributed to PayPal, you need to have conditions in to recognise where the click came from before PayPal. Like PayPal you can exclude Honey tracking to make this simpler. 

Lastly this all only works under the assumption that it's based purely on last click attribution. A lot of affiliate programs will have preferred partners, Linus may get commission no matter where he appears in the click journey. Coupon providers like Honey may also be given their own rate seperate from Linus. They may also set up first click attribution where it's the first click that gets the commission. Or multi touch attribution where both Honey and Linus get a portion of the commission. It's really up to the advertiser how they want their affiliate program to be set up

I say it's not new because advertisers have been navigating these attribution issues since day one of affiliates existing. And if you're relying on affiliate commissions and don't understand this to begin with maybe it's not a space you should be in

Parsing the url to see if there's already an affiliate link in it would require tons of work, especially since you would have to do it for every website that uses affiliate links, so it's a unique check for each. 

So unless theres some additional context in the last 17 mins of the video, the only person getting screwed are the CCs - not the customers? 

Which is nothing new - even youtube does it.

Author: @zalzalahbuttsaab
Content:
Honey, owned by PayPal, is primarily a tool designed to enhance online shopping experiences by helping users find coupons, discounts, and cashback opportunities. For PayPal, the acquisition of Honey serves both strategic and revenue-generating purposes:

Business Purpose for PayPal:

Increase Transaction Volume: By making online shopping more appealing through discounts, Honey encourages users to make purchases, many of which are likely to be completed using PayPal.

Customer Acquisition and Retention: Honey's large user base introduces PayPal to new customers, potentially converting them into regular PayPal users.

Data Insights: Honey provides valuable consumer behavior data, such as shopping preferences, popular products, and purchasing patterns. This helps PayPal improve its services, tailor offers, and strengthen partnerships with merchants.

Merchant Relationships: Honey’s services enhance merchants' ability to target shoppers effectively, making PayPal an indispensable partner in their e-commerce strategies.

How Honey Makes Money:

Affiliate Commissions: Honey earns commissions from merchants for driving sales to their platforms. When a user applies a Honey coupon or cashback offer and completes a purchase, the merchant pays a percentage of the sale to Honey.

Partnerships with Merchants: Honey offers promotional opportunities to merchants, such as exclusive deals, which they pay for to attract more customers.

Data Monetization (Indirect): While Honey doesn’t sell personal data, it aggregates shopping insights to improve PayPal’s ecosystem and merchant offerings.

For PayPal, Honey is both a direct revenue generator through these mechanisms and a strategic asset to maintain its position as a leader in digital payments.

Some YouTubers and critics label Honey as a "scam" or accuse it of being deceptive for the following reasons, though these claims often stem from misunderstandings or exaggerations:

1. Perception of Data Exploitation:

Claim: Honey collects extensive user data (e.g., browsing habits, shopping preferences) and shares or exploits it for profit.

Reality: While Honey does collect data to provide relevant coupons and offers, its privacy policy states that it doesn't sell personal data to third parties. Critics may misconstrue its data collection practices as invasive, raising concerns about user privacy.

2. Inflated Savings or Limited Discounts:

Claim: Honey doesn't always offer the best discounts and sometimes highlights deals that are either outdated, not the lowest price available, or that users could have found independently.

Reality: Coupon codes often expire or don't work universally. Honey relies on crowdsourcing and automated searches, so the results can vary. Critics argue this creates a false sense of savings.

3. Affiliate Commissions Without Transparency:

Claim: Honey earns affiliate commissions for purchases made through its platform, which some feel is not adequately disclosed. Critics may argue this business model incentivizes Honey to promote deals that maximize its profits, rather than focusing solely on benefiting users.

Reality: While this is true, affiliate marketing is a common and legitimate revenue model. However, some users feel misled if they believe Honey's primary purpose is purely altruistic.

4. Potential to Raise Prices Indirectly:

Claim: Honey's partnerships with merchants might lead to artificially inflated "base prices" so that discounts appear more significant than they actually are. Merchants could adjust their pricing strategies to offset the cost of providing discounts through Honey.

Reality: While possible, this accusation largely depends on specific merchant practices, not directly on Honey.

5. Security Concerns:

Claim: Because Honey is a browser extension with access to browsing and shopping activity, critics warn it could be a security risk, especially if it were hacked or misused.

Reality: Honey has safeguards in place, but skepticism is natural when a tool has such broad access.

Conclusion:

The "scam" claims often exaggerate legitimate concerns about transparency, privacy, and effectiveness. Honey operates on a standard affiliate marketing model, but these criticisms highlight the importance of user awareness about how such services function and the trade-offs involved.

Author: @strawhatmikey23
Content: Worked in affiliate industry for YEARS. not only is Honey doing this, but basically all extensions including karma, capital one, rakuten, and many more. Its generally up to the brand or agency to make sure these publishers are setup to where this isnt able to able to happen or that they dont have last click attribution. Its a crazy world. Tons of scamming and bs publishers but the agencies and affiliate teams looks better by showing results from them. So its a “win-win.” If you own a company, be VERY CAREFUL letting coupon sites in your affiliate programs. Even worse…some of the biggest affiliate platforms are the ones running these huge extensions and companies that are scamming lmfao. As an agency or brand…always be transparent. Give honey an exclusive code, and make sure ANY influencer has a better code. Be diligent and scrub all sales from honey that are not specifically their code. This is generally a good way around this and can easily be found in transaction reports if the program is setup correctly.

A YouTube creator, Mega Lag, exposed a significant scam involving the Honey browser extension, owned by PayPal. Despite promoting savings, Honey often fails to find valid discounts or deliberately withholds better deals to benefit partner stores. This deceptive practice has cost creators and consumers millions of dollars and sparked calls for legal action. The investigation highlights Honey's exploitative mechanisms and raises serious ethical and legal concerns.

Author: @JDB-tc5rs
Content:
Affiliate marketer here. This is how industry works. They didn't do anything illegal. "Last Click" attribution is exactly this -> If I refer you to a website, and you reach checkout but abandon it and click a different affiliate link 3 days later, it overrides your affiliate link. This is what "Last Click" entails. Honey did walk a thin line in the gray area by sneakily hiding their own affiliate link inside their extension button, but nothing done here was illegal as there are no specific rules on any affiliate platforms that forbid this. Affiliate marketing is a bit of a wild west, and with enough brain juice, you can cook up some sweet gray-zone ideas to make a bank, without actually breaking the law. Is it morally right? Absolutely not, but it's legally right :)

The salesman analogy isn't quite correct  either. Salesman are people who are hired by a company and operate on a set of rules imposed on all of them -> Affiliate is the same, only we all agree (by choosing "Last Click" attribution) to have our commission taken by another affiliate who got the customer to pay. We steal and we get stolen from. The analogy here is illustrating someone with an unfair advantage, but that's literally how Affiliates work, we all find ways to one up the rest, and if someone one ups us - it's GG WP. Honey did get an unfair advantage by being placed in a browser extension that gives out coupons, but other affiliates could've done so too. This is why I don't mess around with "Last Click" attribution but usually go for "First Click" or "Dynamic" as that's guaranteed to not get overridden. 

Again, a bunch of privacy measures like the ones post iOS14 , and inside Safari completely forbid cookies and UTMs, costing affiliates far more than Honey. Apple literally goes "nope, you can't earn a commission" cuz f*ck you, and everyone celebrated it. I had a 60% income drop-off post iOS14, but you don't see people taking out their pitchforks to defend us.

As for this whole scandal, don't blame Honey - they're just the biggest fish that got caught in the net and used as a scape goat - blame the advertisers (companies that give out affiliate codes without in dept oversight and rules how to properly use them), blame the highly-unregulated affiliate industry, as what's been discussed here is legal, and blame the platforms like Share-a-sale, ClickBank, and similar for not coming up with a fair framework for "Last Click" attribution model.

Author: @pr0xZen
Content:
I really appreciate your content and the quality of character you've demonstrated over the years, and I have faith that you will recognize this criticism for what it is; no more, no less: _I think this reaction piece was posted too early, and that it used and leaned a bit too much on MegaLag's original content for how soon after the original's launch it was posted._ I feel the sum of factors, including your YT channel having _more than _*_30 times_*_ as many subs as MegaLag,_ this moved substantially into the realm of "usurping the market" of his original video.

There is a pretty well established line of ethics/norms for reaction content. And IMO one of the most essential of all is that you give the original creator *_at least (!)_*_ 48 hours after org release,_ before posting reaction content based on it. _Especially_ if your channel/following is substantially larger than that of the original creator and content. And if this is the case (as it most definitely is here), that we are extra sensitive to *at what extent* we retell the whole story and replay its content, the closer to the original contents release we post our recaction type content of it. A "boosting effect" is also involved in this case, but I believe you've already made your views clear about not being supportive of the "paid in exposure" concept. Meaning even if the outcome turns out favorable, even if there is _a bit_ of transformative work - whether it's the explicit intent or not it does not legitimize usurping the market with reaction content.

My impression of your character, your former content and rhetoric, leads me to believe you will at least be understanding of this critique, whether or not you fully agree with this particular instance or its minutae.

Author: @emberkat0000
Content:
Maybe it's because I've been using the internet since 1994, but any of these types of browser extensions and cute little programs have always been a red flag to me. They always used to be scams that would hijack browsers, steal personal info, and when online purchases started, steal card details. To me Honey looked just like another scam from the old days (Emjois started out as a spyware program that tricked people into "upgrading" their emotes) .

As for the stealing of commissions, it's illegal in many countries and may be in some states in America. If they have an agreement with the referrer that includes commissions (through referral links) and the boss switches out your name for their own or another, then it's fraud. If there is no agreement and it's just auto hijacking referral links, then it's straight theft and borderline hacking.

One way they would have been getting around this was offering Honey branded referral links for promoters so they still got paid commissions, and only stealing commissions when users used Honey with a unrelated referral link. Still illegal in some countries but maybe not America. It would have been why promoters who found out, barely said anything as there was nothing they could do as users were the ones essentially changing the referral links by using Honey.

I hope at the very least companies cancel all sales that have honey as the referral, and at the best reclaim the commissions to paypal and Honey is prosecuted. I'm not sure how the people who lost commissions can reclaim unless they have enough proof that Honey was the reason they didn't get paid for sales, but I hope they can come together and get paid properly.

Content:
The worse part is that it's likely that Honey Gold/PayPal Rewards affiliated sites are accomplice of this scam too.
Because the whole point is that it saves them money for a small commisson given to Honey.

With the NordVPN exemple :
NordVPN gained ~25-33$ (by not having to pay the Influencer but paying Honey a way less costly commission instead)
Honey gained the commission price minus the 1$ CashBack
User (you) gained 1$ throught CashBack
Influencer lost 35$

Same idea for not showing the best deals : They control the "coupon" landscape for their affiliated sites so those sites gain more money (by losing less through coupons and affiliated links) and all they need to do is pay is a 3-5% commission which is way more profitable than not doing it. Thus scaming You directly this time.

This is likely to be a multi-company scam, not just Honey.
Honey is the central figure but it's also "just" the middle man for all 40000+ companies willingly in that system. Be aware of that, it's not just Honey.
This is huge (and probably so big it will get buried by under the table money/deals).

Author: @joshuakarchie6945
Content:
Hey Charlie, this video was "Mega DOO DOO".

Look, we all know nothing is truly “free,” right? And when something is offering us a service at no cost, there has to be a way for them to make money to keep it running. Honey is a prime example of this. The extension helps us save money, find discounts, and overall makes shopping online a lot easier. But how does it make money? Through referral links, where they get a small commission when someone makes a purchase after clicking a link Honey provided.

Now, some people feel a little weird about this. It feels sneaky, right? But honestly, it's a pretty common thing online. Tons of websites, bloggers, and influencers use affiliate links—basically, links that earn them a little cash if you click through and make a purchase. Honey is doing the same thing, just in a way that's less obvious. They replace the “referral” cookie with their own to help fund their free service. It’s not like they're tricking you into buying things you don’t need or charging you extra. They're just getting a small cut for helping connect you with discounts.

Here’s the thing—Honey isn’t charging you a dime for the savings you’re getting. They’re not asking for your credit card or subscription fee. They’re offering you a totally free tool to save money. So, if they make a little cash through affiliate links? Honestly, that’s just how the internet works. It’s how a lot of free apps, websites, and services survive and keep giving us good stuff without hitting us with fees.

Plus, let’s be real—no one’s forcing you to use their referral links. You can always opt out or ignore it if it doesn’t sit well with you. But if you’re getting access to better deals and saving money without paying a cent, I’d say that’s a pretty fair trade. And at the end of the day, Honey is just doing what every other business does to keep their services running in a world where “free” rarely means free.

Honey’s not out here trying to pull a fast one on you—they’re just doing what they need to do to keep delivering a service that actually helps people.

Author: @beva901
Content:
Hey all I work for and adtech company and I’m here to say I don’t think this is the gotcha moment you all are thinking. Honey has an adtech platform. First y’all have no idea how they internally track their campaigns. He shouldn’t be looking at campaign names he should be looking at ids which are internally mapped so even then he wouldn’t be able to track the supply chain. Second there are two types of affiliate campaigns CPA (cost per action) and CPC (cost per click). A purchase would be cost per action campaign. So as long as they are being transparent with Linus that he is getting a CPC commission and paying out for that click and then later affiliating the action there is no wrong done here. And this is likely what they’re doing.  That’s probably why they weren’t shy about telling him because that’s how the system works y’all. 
Now if Linus was enrolled in a CPA campaign and they jacked the commission without paying him downstream before expiry (meaning how long the cookie associated with the click from Linus will track the purchase) then that would be a problem. But they have logs of all of these redirect paths. So I doubt they’re doing this. Listen. I hate honey and if it makes you feel any better the industry does too. But adtech is such a complicated beast people shouldn’t be sure they have any idea what’s happening unless they’re recording all of the redirect path and can thoroughly break down the tracking tags which he didn’t do here. And I hate to break to you there is a world where this isn’t illegal and it’s this one. And before y’all come for me this is not how our product works. This is specifically how coupon browser extensions work.

Author: @KYUKIREL
Content:
Using simple logic, we can infer that Honey is neither a good nor sustainable service. Here's an example:

Let’s start by assuming Honey works as advertised: it finds and applies the best of possible discounts for your purchases. While this may seem appealing at firsts, there is a serious flaws, both logically and ethically.

There are two possible scenarios here:

1. The Seller Doesn’t Mind the Discounts
If the seller doesn’t oppose the discounts Honey applies, there are several potential reasons for this:

The discount is insignificant or doesn’t directly impact the seller because the middleman (e.g., Amazon, E-Bay) absorbs the cost.

Worse, the discount may not even be genuine, such as when sellers artificially mark up prices before applying the discount to create the illusion of savings.
In this case, consumers are misled into thinking they’re getting a good deal when, in reality, they’re paying the original price or even more.


2. The Seller Opposes the Discounts
If the seller dislikes the discounts (e.g., because they reduce profits or disrupt targeted promotions), they are likely to adapt by:

Increasing base prices to compensate for the discounts, which affects all consumers, including those who don’t use Honey.

Reducing the availability of genuine coupons, undermining the purpose of discounts as targeted tools for rewarding specific consumer groups.

This scenario harms everyone: prices rise overall, and the value of discounts diminishes. In both cases, the market is distorted, and consumers—both Honey users and non-users—bear the brunt of the consequences.
--- 
Another perspective on the long-term impact of Honey's service is its potential to create a system with Ponzi-scheme-like dynamics:

Over time, Honey’s system creates a market dynamic resembling a Ponzi scheme. Early users benefit from discounts before the market adjusts, but as retailers adapt by increasing prices, later users and non-users are penalized. The “discounts” eventually become meaningless, as they merely bring prices back to what would have been the baseline in a fair market.

Author: @Exachad
Content:
I'm shocked it took this long to break the news because people knew about this a long time ago. Although I may be biased because I cofounded a shopping related Chrome extension in college (not an unethical one), but it was obvious to me that Honey was making most of its money from dubious use of affiliate links despite not referring anyone to the sites they trigger the affiliate on. There's obviously no money to be made from just entering discount codes on sites, let alone enough to justify a $4 billion valuation, which is just common sense.

Affiliate links are the only mechanism through which shopping related chrome extensions can generate decent money, and all these shady cashback apps use it even in cases where they don't refer anyone to the site. The real mystery to me has always been why Amazon and other big sites tolerate these extensions triggering their affiliate links and taking a cut of their money without referring anyone there. They should ban them from their affiliate program because they're only costing them money.

Author: @TheAcenightcreeper
Content:
I posted about this in reddit years ago, im a certifed fraud examiner and a certified anti money laundering specialist.  I have been in the industry for 20 years, worked for large payment organizations… i had made complaints into the FTC, separate from my day job… shortly after honey was first purchased by Paypal. This was known years ago by people who were familiar with paypal, who were part of this rollout…


One only needs to ask “how does honey make money” to understand why this is occuring.  If you see the original functionality, honey was based on adverts and product/coupon selection. The original complaints about honey were related to better coupon codes being available than what honey was finding.  Prior to the purchase of honey, the program still didnt find you the “best” coupon codes, this is what i first noticed and why i filed my original complaint with the FTC.  

But thats not what paypal saw as the main value of honey when they purchased it. I cant get into all the details, but I know for certain that  within that organization, This was the entire plan with the purchase of honey and was something discussed during the due diligence prior to the buyout.  This was touted as a feature that honey was touting as a means to become profitable, but they never got comfortable with it from a legal perspective…
I promise you this will come out in the discovery phase of the lawsuits.  This was very deliberate and how paypal planned to monetize their purchase of this plugin that was not worth $4billion in its original form, it was not a profitable business.  I cannot get into additional details, but i can tell you, that this will be larger than civil lawsuits.  The FTC will eventually be involved

Author: @ArifBillahOnGoogle
Content:
*Web dev here:* be cautious of using browser extensions in general. A browser extension is essentially an "almighty spy", regardless of what extension it is. They have access to EVERY BIT of the code that's used to show you web pages on ANY website. So, if this HUGE power falls in the wrong hands, they can do ANYTHING you can. Passwords, card info, things you type, pages you visit, clicking and visiting pages on your behalf, literally ANYTHING and EVERYTHING is just a few lines of code away for them!

That's why I make my own extensions whenever possible. Remember there was this "Copy link text" extension I used use for a long time but once investigated into their source code and found a file containing how many lines of literal "spying" code???? Make a guess.... 40,000 lines!!! Yes! And it should have been less than 100 lines to "Copy link text"! That extension is now removed from Chrome Store, but I have a local copy just for reference.

I don't mean to drive you off of extensions all together, but just remember, if you install the wrong extension, you get screwed REAL BAD!

Content: Calling it now, at 21:03 that the reason you would randomly get a good deal and sometimes let the person get their affiliate link commission is similar to why there is still a minimum win percentage on a lot machine. But if Honey rarely and randomly gives you a 60% off coupon, sure someone might lose more money on that one sale, but it keeps you the user invested that there is a chance that it works so you keep using it. I’m sure with the affiliate link side, if you get X amount of clicks and $0, it might be a lot easier to find Honey as the culprit, but if it randomly lets transactions slide, then you’ll still see transactions post on your end and maybe you’ll think “oh, maybe that many people aren’t clicking this particular link”. A coupon is a referral. Because the only way to get it is to get advertised to by someone who worked with the original company to make a valid coupon.
You don’t believe a random string of numbers magically makes things cheap? Do you?
Coupons are marketing and are referrals to start with.

Coupon codes always have overridden influencer links. That’s how it has always been.
Please be careful calling this bad, because nothing bad has happened here.

Content: It's not really a scam in a way, at least no more then a scam as a street salesman selling you a newspaper subscription. On the influencer side I would assume they get paid for endorsing Honey. Is it scummy that they potentially break any future deals the influencer gets from other partnerships, of course it is. The fact Honey seemed pretty open when asked questions about it. Makes me wonder shouldn't the influencers be responsible on researching a company before accepting deals from them that seemed to good to be true? On the consumer side they willingly install the add-on, where there influenced or just found the company by chance doesn't change anything about that fact. The fact is Honey does exactly what it promises it gets you the best deal. As explained in the video company's maybe don't want you to use that 20% coupon, so you get the 10% coupon. At that point you do get the best deal a company wants to offer on a certain product. Keep in mind a company has to deal with certain profit margins that vary on the product type. So I can imagine a company willing to give 10% discount on product A, and maybe 20% on product B, also add the commission Honey makes from the sale. This reduces the profit margin from a company by a lot. This makes me wonder has this been tested, using Honey on different products on the same website? So is it a scam, no don't think so. Is it somewhat scummy, yes it is. But I also believe it's common sense you look into something before you blindly install it on your system. 👀

Author: @oxtailsoup6493
Content:
If PayPal is doing this through honey which is a separate browser extension, how do we know PayPal isn’t also doing this when you pay for a product through the PayPal link in the checkout page of almost any consumer webpage. 

On almost every single website when you go to your cart to check out there are almost always multiple options with which to check out and PayPal is almost always among one of the check out options. 

When you choose to pay for the product on a checkout page through PayPal it redirects you to log in to your PayPal account to approve your purchase and the method of using PayPal (for example paying directly from your bank account, paying from a debit card you have already added to PayPal, or using your PayPal credit card on your account). 

Once you’ve chosen the method of PayPal payment you want to use for purchase, PayPal re-directs you back to the consumer website to finalize the transaction. The point is, in this scenario, PayPal is the “last click” in the chain and could easily swap their own affiliate code for the original that brought you to the consumer website to begin with (or create a brand new one if you didn’t reach the website through a prior affiliate) when you choose to pay via your PayPal account regardless if you have honey installed on your cpu or not. 

What if the reason why PayPal bought honey wasn’t because they solely wanted to use that particular plugin to steal affiliate money but also because they wanted to integrate the “last click replacement technology” that honey represented, into their own PayPal redirect purchasing option that is included in almost every single consumer website on the internet? 

I guess what I’m saying here is that it would make a lot more sense for PayPal to purchase honey for 4 billion dollars if their end goal was to incorporate the “last click technology” that honey uses into every single PayPal purchase option on every single consumer website that they already have access to. This isn’t about honey being a scam, this is about the PayPal check out option that is ubiquitous on the internet becoming the sole beneficiary of every single affiliate purchase commission every time someone decides they want to use their PayPal account as a means of purchasing a product online, regardless of whether they have honey installed or not…

…I’m not suicidal.

Author: @a---------------
Content:
Man, even I was fooled since I had this extension since I was so young and didn't even think about it til now. I realized as I got older that when looking at a business, the first thing you have to ask yourself is "How do they monetize/make money exactly?". Especially for a company that seems that it would lose money like Honey, how does an extension that gives discounts generate any income exactly? And if you can't find an answer, then there is most likely some nefarious business practices going on to generate their revenue. 


Here's the thing though. Honey will not be sued because this is technically legal.

No Direct Deception: Honey's core function is to find coupons and cashback. It's not directly misrepresenting what it does, even if its other actions, like replacing affiliate links, is not transparent.

User Agreement: Users generally agree to Honey's terms of service, which may outline the possibility of link replacement. While this might be buried in the fine print, it still forms the basis of the legal relationship.

Competition: Honey's actions could be viewed as competitive business practices rather than direct fraud. They are a third party inserting themselves into the customer purchase process.

Technically, a user is not entitled to the commission the creator is entitled to, and the user may not even know which creator they originally received the link from. Thus, replacing the link is not technically fraudulent as it still gets a user to the same, or lower price.

Let me be the devil's advocate and ask, how else do you expect Honey to work? Say I go to an online store without any referral or affiliate link and just bought something using Honey's service and found a discount code. How would the online store know I used Honey service? Author: @KarateofComedy
Content:
Yeah, I knew this was happening. I guess it comes with the territory of knowing how computers work. I can see how many people didn't understand, but here's a good rule of thumb for everyone out there. On the internet, if something is free, you're the product. That might mean you are selling your attention, your data, or in this case, your cookies, but you're selling something. The internet doesn't run for free.

I don't think the lawsuit has legs.
You gave full cookies permissions to them when you got the add-on... and they used them... and they told you how they were using them. The customer themself authorized the automated change of cookie.
 
One could argue that they are withholding the best coupons from the customer and not delivering to the best of their ability... but since when has that ever been the standard by which the law steps in? I get sh!tty service from lots of places.
 
Ultimately, the customer allowed this application on their browser, they approved it, they were provided all of the information about how it works, and the customer either lied about reading the terms and conditions, or they didn't care that they passed the commissions over to honey instead of the affiliate.
 
Legally speaking... I don't think this case really has legs. The customer-side is entitled to NOTHING, and the affiliate side... so sorry, but the customer sold you out for nothing. At the end of the day, I guess the affiliate side can sue, but the best they'll get is a quiet settlement.

Author: @aurawilming6047
Content:
People tend to over estimate how much "our data" is actually worth. Yes, it is a business, I am not denying that. But it's not a "I'm going to sponsor hundreds of influencers" amount of money just selling data that boils down to consumer habits. The players who do make money on selling your data will never think of spending on sponsoring and commercials. They will just quietly make deals with Facebook or Google or something. Mark was right looking at the money spent (even if the amounts were never disclosed) vs money gained and say "something isn't adding up".
And those who are comparing this to the Better Help scandal, Better Help never set out to scam people, they just didn't vet the parties offering services via their platform. They tried to give the impression of some sort of medical board while in reality it was more of a therapy Craigslist. Some of it was great, some of it was horrible and the user had no way of telling which was which until it was too late. That's not a failing of the model, that's a failing of execution.

Author: @ryanwhittaker1201
Content:
I’ve been in the affiliate advertising industry for a long time and knew they operated like this. Early on in their operations though, they operated on a first touch basis, not last touch, so their affiliate code would only track people who were “organic” and not going to provide any commissions. With a first touch conversion model, it makes perfect sense, but in a last touch model its literally stealing.

This has always been their model and how they make money and admittedly, they’ve never hid it. But its worth noting that attribution is up to the product. A company like Nord needs to allow Honey to register as an affiliate and also provide them with a last touch attribution model to get them paid. Product company’s ignorance on their affiliate program allowed this.

Author: @ilyafoskin
Content: I always assumed Honey made money by selling the sales data they collect. They have their program sitting in the browser with access to what is bought, which kinds of people buy what, where things are bought, etc. I figured webscraping for coupons was an easy enough thing to do for them to become a trojan horse and get on your browser. I'm sure they also do that but their real business model really is nefariously clever. Once someone downloads Honey, the company steal the affiliate money of everyone whose affiliate link the person uses. That aspect I can kind of respect. They found a niche way to basically scoop up free money using a little known quirk of online selling and it's probably legal. I expect it slots into a grey area under the law where it's not technically stealing and they had no obligation to disclose it because the last point of sale system doesn't guaranteed priority to any one affiliate. But the way they let businesses actually prevent them from finding the best coupon deals is unforgivable. That's lying to the customer on the fundamental selling point of their whole service.

Author: @ChibiQilin
Content:
It's fascinating how after a decade+ of influencers telling other influencers (and their audiences) "I don't blame anybody for grabbing that bag, take whatever sponsorships you can" we now see time and again the consequences of that. VPNs overselling what they do, fake lord/lady titles, scam products, energy drinks aimed at people who are mostly sedentary, etc.

At some point, you have to hold influencers responsible for what they're telling their audience to buy. Influencers have been shouting "this is a real job" for well over a decade, and now they're making more money than most small businesses do. But when they're negligent, it's never their fault. Scam sponsorships are practically no different than scam crypto coins, other than the creator just gets a bigger cut of the pie and are more involved. But really they should be responsible.

Literally anybody who's tech competent knows to avoid honey. Now they probably had no idea about the referral swap, but pretty much anybody even moderately tech competent would assume it's at least harvesting user data to resell. These kinds of things make money somehow, and when they spend so much on sponsorships, that makes it even more untrustworthy. This is another example among dozens of creators pushing a shady product onto their audience, then doing a pikachu face when it turns out the shady product was shadier than we realized.

Author: @regidice
Content:
As someone who worked in affiliate marketing for around 5 years this is called last click attribution.

It’s not done by design by affiliate partners like honey, but by the affiliate platforms themselves (rakuten, partnerize, amazon affiliates, etc).
It’s the only way for them to know who to pay out the commission to - the last affiliate link click before checkout.
It happens way more often than you could imagine and is often a pain point for many that work in the industry.

A common example of this is using a cashback site and clicking through those links to earn money back, searching for an extra discount code online and copying that code to apply at checkout.
You’ve just redirected the commission payout to whoever owns that affiliate code rather than the cashback company.

Yes it’s a deceptive practice to have that coupon extension pop up even if nothing is on offer, I doubt that a class action would get very far.
They’ll likely be forced to change the logic of the extension to only appear when a coupon is applicable as the actual practice itself isn’t illegal.

Author: @metazare
Content:
I'm not able to find any sympathy for influencers affected by this. These types of browser extensions have been around since the early 2000's, at the very least. They never do anything good. The list of negative things these types of programs and extensions have done in the past is well documented. Browser hijackers, data scraping, spyware, ad injectors to name a few. 

Any influencer who hocked this thing for the promise of money should have known better than to promote it. This should have never been promoted because of the very nature of what it is. The ramifications of using something like this can range from trivial, to catastrophic. For those who argue "How could I have known?" These are the kinds of scams our parents and grandparents fell for when the internet was still in its infancy. If you as an adult influencer were tricked by this then you have a severe lack of critical thinking power, and everyone should be very skeptical about anything you promote because you're not smart enough to sniff out an obvious scam or something potentially dangerous.

Author: @RyguyAB
Content:
I'm not going to pretend that I couldn't get caught up by something like this, but I do have to say that the part about Honey scamming its users by not actually going and finding the best coupons is basically what I assumed from the first time I heard about it.  I thought that if  there wasn't something like this going on, where they were basically colluding with e-tailers to control the coupons, they would have functionally no model to earn revenue because they aren't charging users their own fees and there is no reason for an e-tailer to work with them UNLESS they were finding a way to either bring enough unique visitors to the website to overcome any loss of margin (which doesn't appear to be their model at all), or they were actively limiting the impact of coupon savings on the margin if the e-tailers by limiting the coupons that Honey would actually have access to (or display) to users. 

I actually realize now that, in theory there was another possible way that Honey could have been making money without scamming their users, as I would never have thought of the "stealing commissions" from their advertising partners and, in theory,, they could potentially have had a more legitimate model if, for example, paypal charged lower transaction fees to e-tailers who agreed to have Honey able to scrape their coupons without the more nefarious action after also allowing them to dictate which coupons could show up.  

At any rate, my point is probably that I was saved more by cynicism than by smarts, so it's good to be a misanthrope?!? 😂

Author: @oxdaman1
Content:
As wild as this is, I can't feel much sympathy for the influencers who worked with Honey or the people who use it. For the former, despite stating that "Honey gets the commission for doing nothing", because they're sponsoring the people they're working with (i.e. paying them an agreed upon amount in the four digits or more usually), that's technically more effort than the influencer's part, which is usually comprises mentioning the sponsor  during their streams, slapping a logo on their overlay, or maybe pre-recording a sponsor segment to stick in their videos. It sucks that they were scammed out of money they could have made, but they still made more than enough to be content this entire time. 

And for the people who use Honey to begin with, that's literally their fault for being scammed. It's less a matter of praying on ignorance, but more so on laziness. I mean think about it: what business would partner with a company in order to make less money via finding the best coupons for consumers ? I suppose the counter point to that would be such coupons being the make or break of a sale, but the businesses don't really need a third party to do that and just post such deals where everyone can see them. 

I suppose a lawsuit could be brought up on the grounds of "false advertising," but the issue there is that the scam has technically been out in the open this whole time in that it clearly pops up on the browser, it's written on their page, and support even openly admits this. It just prays on people not knowing how affiliate links work via browsers and, again, people's laziness when it comes to searching for coupons themselves. 

So yeah. Wild stuff, but ultimately, for both the influencers and consumers, it's their own fault for being scammed in the first place.

Author: @Volcanron
Content:
WAIT. NOW THEY'RE BACK AT IT AGAIN WITH A DIFFERENT SERVICE.

Just 2 days ago, I saw that YouTube got around uBlock again. I decided "screw it, I'll just watch for now and figure it out later." The very first ad I saw was for Pie, an adblock. I decided I'd go to it and check it out. They said on the site that they block ads from all sites, including YouTube and even Twitch, which not even uBlock could do. So I decided to download the extension, and sure enough it worked. Yippee me.

Fast forward to today, and I see this video in my sub feed while on my phone. Decide I'll get to it later. Watch a different video, they play an ad for Pie again. I watch it, curious if it could get around the app too. Obviously it can't, but it did say something interesting at the end of it: made by the people behind Honey. Okay, now I'm worried. I start watching this video, wondering how Pie fits into this. And I think I got it.

When you download Pie, they have two options for display's sake: a mode that entirely hides ads (like any other sensible adblock), and one where you can watch the ads disappear… which is turned on by default. I think that when you have that on, they try to open those ads to get crediting for them. I immediately turned that mode off so I can't verify it. What I can verify, in some capacity, is this next part.

Remember how I mentioned it could block ads on Twitch? Well, when it does that, it does something rather interesting: it creates a blue ring around the stream (the app color), and tells you how much time they've blocked where the ad timer normally would be. It works perfectly well aside from this, as you can hear the stream audio and everything. But I think it isn't actually blocking the ads. It's playing them somewhere in the background, getting the Adsense instead of the streamer.

I have no means to accurately verify whether my claims are true or not, but I do think that this may be worth looking into further. For everyone I hope I'm wrong, however.

Author: @afs8491
Content: This isn't a scam, it's common practice in the affiliate space. Honey isn't the only coupon site thay does this, Rakuten does too. Influencers/content creators are made aware when signing a deal and must do their due diligence before agreeing (read the terms). This is why influencers/content creators get a lump sum payment + possible commission via affiliate. It is normal behavior for Honey to be paid out as last click in this case. Is it ethical? Absolutely not. Is it transparent? Clearly not, as even Charlie (who has worked with them in the past) was completely unaware. Coupon sites should share the wealth with influencers/content creators in a more ethical manner. I don't believe any lawsuit will hold up here, but I'd love to be proven wrong.

Author: @MicrocosmTheCatboy
Content:
This has done billions of dollars in damage, not millions. Several sponsorships require the creator to get a certain amount of sales with their affiliate link to reach their goals and receive a secondary, vastly larger payment. If Honey is taking the credit, that will completely tank the creators' affiliate link sales, meaning they could fail to hit their goal and damage their reputation with that brand and potentially with other brands. Another factor is that if a company sees its YouTube sponsorships aren't getting enough affiliate sales, they could completely withdraw from YouTube and quit sponsoring creators.

Honey's existence hurts creators and sponsors, which hurts YouTube. Honey will probably be wiped from the Chrome store, and Google will likely sue Honey.

Author: @lewdacario
Content:
Defamation or Slander: If the video makes false claims about a specific person or company, such as accusing them of committing illegal actions without proof, it could potentially be considered defamatory. Defamation involves making false statements that damage the reputation of a person or entity. However, if the claims are true and backed by evidence, it might fall under the realm of free speech or investigative journalism.

Copyright Issues: If MegaLag uses copyrighted content (e.g., clips, images, or music) without permission, the video could face copyright infringement issues. However, this depends on the specific content used and whether it falls under fair use.

Misleading Advertising: If the video is promoting a scam or spreading misinformation about a legitimate influencer marketing practice (such as honey influencers), it could violate consumer protection laws. However, if it's simply exposing fraud, and the information is truthful and well-researched, it would likely be protected speech.

Privacy Violations: If the video includes private or confidential information about individuals without consent, it could be violating privacy laws.

To summarize, unless the video involves defamation, false claims, or privacy violations, it is not necessarily illegal. If it is a critique based on truth and well-supported evidence, it is more likely to be legal. If you have specific concerns about the content of the video, reviewing it in detail or seeking legal advice would be important.

Content: I did almost this *exact* scheme when I was a teenager. Then one day an in-store security guard came to my till to buy his lunch and happened to notice the number that flashed up on the screen was different to his own reward card. Author: @tandiir8334
Content:
100% agree this looks sleazy, but not sure a lawsuit against Honey for this will necessarily be a slam dunk. The only reason I think this won’t be a super easy win for people on the wrong end of Honey’s scheme is that this relates to a long-time and still ongoing limitation in marketing that marketers have been aware of but unable to solve for a long time: marketing attribution. Basically, it’s really hard to explain why people decide to buy a product. They may have tons of touch points with a brand and a product before deciding to buy. It’s really hard to say which of those touch points deserves the most credit because you can’t read customers’ minds.

I think in the case Charlie’s describing, it’s fair to say the affiliates referring their audience to the product did the vast majority do the work to get the buyer to purchase, but I don’t think you can successfully argue Honey did “none” of the work. Their dumb little song and dance about coupon codes likely provides the customer with some small bit of extra confidence to pull the trigger because Honey is convincing the customer (or at least trying to) that they’re getting “the best deal” possible. Doing that job likely deserves some of the credit for making the sale happen, if only a small bit.

Now it seems from the video Honey is basically taking 100% of the credit and getting paid 100% of the referral commission when they’re likely doing very little of the work. That still makes what they’re doing shady and has still likely resulted in millions of dollars lost that rightfully belong to the affiliate partners making these referrals.

I think they’ll try to use the whole marketing attribution argument in court to try to wiggle out of this or reduce the settlement/damages.

EDIT:

Just finished the video. Taking credit for the sale when you click “got it” is especially egregious. They’ll have a very hard time defending that scenario. Ridiculous.

Author: @RyneLanders
Content:
I thought this was pretty common knowledge. Honey makes money in 2 ways: affiliate commissions, and selling your browsing data. Given the first is the most obvious way they make money, of course they're claiming the commission for the sale. It works the exact same way as if you looked up a product review, read 2-3 reviews, and you clicked a link to the product page (e.g., the Amazon links on affiliate review sites that never show the prices but only have the "click to see price" buttons) - the first click is going to get credit for the sale, until the later clicks come in.

I work in online advertising and analytics dealing with affiliates, ad tracking, etc. and this is common. When you get to a checkout page and you see the coupon section, and then you quickly Google a coupon code and get routed to one of those many coupon spam sites, they are doing exactly this. This is why coupon sites that get affiliate commissions are almost 100% wasted revenue for the shop because they didn't bring any value in getting the user there and they claim credit that someone else should have got. All that Honey did was take that step out of the way by convincing you to install their browser and then they auto-fill the discount code that the coupon sites provide on their site. 

Of course the much more nefarious purpose (and the real reason PayPal bought them) is that they now have unlimited access to all of your click stream data in the same way that Facebook has with their 3rd party pixel on every site in the world. That allows PayPal to build up extremely detailed segmentation and user models for everyone that has the extension, and then they sell that data to the data brokers like Axciom/InfoUSA, Yext, etc, the credit bureaus, digital fingerprinting services, and interested governments. Anyone using these has fallen for an obvious trap.

Content:
I don't understand how this seems to be such a huge "wozwer, geez, how could they" moment.

Like... Honey literally tells you what it does IF you read their EULA
Sure, no one does that, but.... you can't call it an illegal scam, if Honey actually asks you to sign a contract with them.

That real life example of TV salesman is fitting, but it ain't Honey's fault, if a customer agrees to fuck over the prior sales guy.

Is it shady?
Sure.
Is it illegal?
No more illegal than people asking you to join a pyramid scheme.

At the end of the day, people have just gotten to comfortable simply clicking everything away on their screens (hence MegaLabs example of "Honey poppe, yadda yadda, click on it to make it go away").

From a business viewpoint, Honey made an extremly clever PR move.

Also, LMG just suddenly "switching" to Karma was most likely them trying to "support" (read as get in on the business) a competitor to this open, easy to access "market".


tl;dr: Honey is shady as fuck, but so are pyramid schemes and sadly both are perfectly legal and rely on people not reading contracts.

Author: @dominiquesmith5839
Content:
Did you know that using rebate extensions like Honey can actually change the price of items?

One Christmas, I was shopping online with my daughter (who lives in my town) and my mother (who lives in another state). For every single item, the prices displayed on my device were higher than those shown to my daughter and mother. They had to purchase the items for me because I was consistently seeing higher prices. After reading the fine print, I discovered that these rebate companies can indeed alter the prices of items. On sites like BestBuy, I was being charged up to $50 more for the same items my daughter and mother were seeing at lower prices.

This revelation floored me! I immediately removed all the extensions and never looked back, even leaving money in my old accounts. I realized then that these companies were essentially scamming me. I thought others knew too, but it seems like many are still unaware.
